# dplyr Basics {#dplyr-basics}

## Introduction

According to a 2016 [CrowdFlower survey](https://www.forbes.com/sites/gilpress/2016/03/23/data-preparation-most-time-consuming-least-enjoyable-data-science-task-survey-says/) reported by [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/), data scientists spend most of their 
time cleaning and manipulating data rather than mining or modeling it for 
insights. As such, we need tools that make data 
manipulation faster and easier. In this chapter, we introduce 
[dplyr](http://dplyr.tidyverse.org/), a grammar of data manipulation.

```{r img1a, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/crowd_flower.png")
```

We will use the following R packages:

```{r libs, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
```

## dplyr Verbs

dplyr provides a set of verbs that help us solve the most common data 
manipulation challenges while working with tabular data (dataframes, tibbles):

- `select`
- `filter`
- `arrange`
- `mutate`
- `summarise`

## Data

```{r showa, message=FALSE}
ecom <- 
  read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy-publications/datasets/master/web.csv',
    col_types = cols_only(device = col_factor(levels = c("laptop", "tablet", "mobile")),
      referrer = col_factor(levels = c("bing", "direct", "social", "yahoo", "google")),
      purchase = col_logical(), n_pages = col_double(), n_visit = col_double(), 
      duration = col_double(), order_value = col_double(), order_items = col_double()
    )
  )

ecom
```

### Data Dictionary

Below is the description of the data set:

- referrer: referrer website/search engine
- device: device used to visit the website
- n_pages: number of pages visited
- duration: time spent on the website (in seconds)
- purchase: whether visitor purchased
- order_value: order value of visitor (in dollars)
- n_visit: number of visits


## Case Study

We will use dplyr to answer the following:

- what is the average order value by device types?
- what is the average number of pages visited by purchasers and non-purchasers?
- what is the average time on site for purchasers vs non-purchasers?
- what is the average number of pages visited by purchasers and non-purchasers 
using mobile?


## Average Order Value

```{r img2a, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/image.jpg")
```


## AOV by Devices

:::{.callout-tip}
## Reading pipes

`|>` forwards the tibble on its left into the first
argument of the verb on its right (see the Preface primer). Every verb below
returns a tibble, so the chain reads as one sentence: keep purchasers,
summarise revenue and orders by device, add AOV, keep two columns, sort.
:::

```{r case}
ecom |>
  filter(purchase) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(order_value), orders = n(), .by = device) |>
  mutate(
    aov = revenue / orders
  ) |>
  select(device, aov) |>
  arrange(aov)
```

## Syntax

Before we start exploring the dplyr verbs, let us look at their syntax:

- the first argument is always a `data.frame` or `tibble`
- the subsequent arguments provide the information required for the verbs to 
take action
- the name of columns in the data need not be surrounded by quotes


## Filter Rows

To compute the AOV, we must first separate the purchasers from 
the non-purchasers. We do this with the `filter()` function, which keeps the
rows that meet a specific condition. The first argument is the name of the data
frame and the rest are expressions for filtering the data. Let us look at a 
few examples:

The first example filters all visits from device **mobile**. As 
we learned in the previous section, the first argument is our data set `ecom` 
and the next is the condition for filtering rows.

```{r img4bb, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/filter_1.png")
```

```{r dplyr2}
filter(ecom, device == "mobile")
```

We can specify multiple filtering conditions as well. In the example below, we
specify two filter conditions:

- visit from device **mobile**
- resulted in a purchase or conversion

```{r img5a, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/filter_2.png")
```

```{r dplyr3}
filter(ecom, device == "mobile", purchase)
```

Here is another example where we specify multiple conditions: 

- visit from device **tablet**
- made a purchase
- browsed less than 15 pages 

```{r dplyr4}
filter(ecom, device == "tablet", purchase, n_pages < 15)
```

### Case Study

Let us apply what we have learned to the case study. We want to filter all
visits that resulted in a purchase. 

```{r dplyr5}
filter(ecom, purchase)
```

## Select Columns

After filtering the data, we need to select the relevant variables to compute the 
AOV. Remember, we do not need every column in the data to compute the metric 
we need. The `select()` function keeps a subset 
of columns. The first argument is the name of the data frame and the subsequent 
arguments specify the columns by name or position. 

To select the `device` and `duration` columns, we specify the data set, 
`ecom`, followed by the column names.

```{r img6a, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/select_1.png")
```

```{r dplyr6}
select(ecom, device, duration)
```

We can select a set of columns using `:`. In the example below, we select all 
the columns starting from `referrer` up to `order_items`. Remember that we can use `:` only when
the columns are adjacent in the data set.


```{r img7a, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/select_2.png")
```

```{r dplyr7}
select(ecom, referrer:order_items)
```

What if you want to select all the columns except a few? Typing the names of many
columns can be cumbersome and may also result in spelling errors. We may use `:`
only if the columns are adjacent, but that may not always be
the case. dplyr allows us to drop columns using `-`. In the example below, we
select all columns except `n_pages` and 
`duration`. Notice the `-` before both of them.

```{r img8a, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/select_3.png")
```

```{r dplyr8}
select(ecom, -n_pages, -duration)
```

### Case Study

For our case study, we need to select the column `order_value`
to calculate the AOV. We also need to select the `device` column as we are 
computing the AOV for each device type.

```{r dplyr9}
select(ecom, device, order_value)
```

But we want the above data only for purchasers. Let us combine `filter()` and 
`select()` to keep `device` and `order_value` only for the
visits that resulted in a purchase.

```{r dplyr10}
# filter all visits that resulted in a purchase
ecom1 <- filter(ecom, purchase)

# select the relevant columns
ecom2 <- select(ecom1, device, order_value)

# view data
ecom2
```

## Grouping Data

We need the total revenue and the number of orders for each device 
to compute their AOV. To achieve this, we need to group the selected `order_value` by device
type. `group_by()` groups 
or splits data based on a particular (discrete) variable. The first argument is the 
name of the data set and the second is the column to split 
the data by. 

To split the data by referrer type, we use `group_by` and specify the data set,
`ecom`, and the column to split by, `referrer`.

```{r dplyr11}
group_by(ecom, referrer)
```

### Case Study

In the second line of the output above, you can observe `Groups: referrer [5]`
. The data is split into 5 groups as the referrer variable has 5 distinct values. 
For our case study, we need to group the data by `device` type.

```{r dplyr12}
# split ecom2 by device type
ecom3 <- group_by(ecom2, device)
ecom3
```

## Summarise Data

The next step is to compute the total revenue and the number of orders for each 
device, i.e. we need to reduce the order value data to a single 
summary. We can achieve this using `summarise()`. As usual, the first argument 
is the name of a data set and the subsequent arguments are functions that 
summarise data. For example, we can use `min`, `max`, `sum`, `mean` etc.

Let us compute the average number of pages browsed by referrer type:

- split data by `referrer` type
- compute the average number of pages using `mean`

```{r img10a, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/groupby_summarise.png")
```

```{r sumeg}
# split data by referrer type
step_1 <- group_by(ecom, referrer)

# compute average number of pages
step_2 <- summarise(step_1, mean(n_pages))
step_2
```

Now let us compute both the `mean` and the `median`.

```{r sumeg2}
# split data by referrer type
step_1 <- group_by(ecom, referrer)

# compute average number of pages
step_2 <- summarise(step_1, mean(n_pages), median(n_pages))
step_2
```

The two steps above, split with `group_by()` and then `summarise()`, can also be
written in one step with the `.by` argument, which groups only for that verb
and leaves the data ungrouped afterwards:

```{r sumeg_by}
# compute average number of pages by referrer without group_by()
step_2 <- summarise(ecom, mean(n_pages), median(n_pages), .by = referrer)
step_2
```

One difference to know: `group_by()` sorts the result by group, while `.by`
keeps the rows in order of first appearance. Use `arrange()` afterwards when
the order matters.

Another way to summarise the order value is to use
`across()` inside `summarise()`. AOV is a per-order metric, so we start from
the purchasers in `ecom1`. `across()` applies the summary
function to all the columns in the data set except the grouping
column. We therefore need to ensure that the data does not have any
irrelevant columns.

- split data by `referrer` type
- select `referrer` and `order_value`
- compute the average order value by applying the `mean` function to all 
the columns


```{r sumall_eg}
# select relevant columns
step_1 <- select(ecom1, referrer, order_value)

# split data by referrer type
step_2 <- group_by(step_1, referrer)

# compute average order value by referrer
step_3 <- summarise(step_2, across(everything(), mean))
step_3
```

Let us compute the `mean` and `median` order value for each referrer type using
`summarise()` with `across()`.

```{r sumall_eg2}
# select relevant columns
step_1 <- select(ecom1, referrer, order_value)

# split data by referrer type
step_2 <- group_by(step_1, referrer)

# compute mean and median order value
step_3 <- summarise(step_2, across(everything(), list(mean = mean, median = median)))
step_3
```

### Case Study

So far, we have split the data by `device` type and we have selected 2 
columns, `device` and `order_value`. We need the total revenue and the number of
orders. What functions can we use to obtain them? The `sum()` function will 
generate the sum of the values and `n()` will count the rows, so we use
them inside the `summarise()` function. Remember, we need to provide a name for
each summary being generated. 

```{r dplyr13}
ecom4 <- summarise(ecom3, revenue = sum(order_value),
          orders = n())
ecom4
```

There you go, we have the total revenue and the number of orders for each
device type. The same grouped summary can be written more directly with
the `.by` argument, which avoids keeping the data grouped with
`group_by()`/`ungroup()`:

```{r dplyr14}
ecom4 <- summarise(ecom2, revenue = sum(order_value), orders = n(), .by = device)
ecom4
```

## Create Columns

To create a new column, we will use `mutate()`. The first argument is the name 
of the data set and the subsequent arguments are expressions for creating new 
columns based on existing columns. 

Let us add a new column `avg_page_time` i.e. time on site divided by the number
of pages visited.

```{r mutateg}
# select duration and n_pages from ecom
mutate_1 <- select(ecom, n_pages, duration)
mutate(mutate_1, avg_page_time = duration / n_pages)
```

We can create new columns from other columns created using `mutate`. Let us 
create another column, `sqrt_avg_page_time`, the square root of the average time
on page using `avg_page_time`.

```{r mutateg2}
mutate(mutate_1,
       avg_page_time = duration / n_pages,
       sqrt_avg_page_time = sqrt(avg_page_time))
```

### Case Study

Back to our case study: from the last step we have the total revenue and the
number of orders for each device category, so we can compute the AOV. We will 
create a new column to store it. 

```{r img11, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/mutate_1.png")
```

```{r dplyr15}
ecom5 <- mutate(ecom4, aov = revenue / orders)
ecom5
```

The last step is to select the relevant columns. We keep the device type 
and the corresponding aov and drop the rest. Use `select()`
to extract the relevant columns.

```{r dplyr16}
ecom6 <- select(ecom5, device, aov)
ecom6
```

## Arrange Data

Arranging data in ascending or descending order is one of the most common tasks
in data manipulation. We can use `arrange` to arrange data by different columns.
Let us say we want to arrange data by the number of pages browsed.

```{r img13, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/arrange_1.png")
```

```{r arrange_eg}
arrange(ecom, n_pages)
```

If we want the data in descending order, we use `desc()`:

```{r arrange_eg2}
arrange(ecom , desc(n_pages))
```

Data can be arranged by multiple variables as well. Let us arrange the data first by 
number of visits and then by number of pages in descending order.

```{r arrange_eg3}
arrange(ecom, n_visit, desc(n_pages))
```

### Case Study

`ecom6` is in device order; sort it by `aov`:

```{r arrange4}
arrange(ecom6, aov)
```

## AOV by Devices

Let us combine all the code from the above steps:

```{r dplyr17}
ecom1 <- filter(ecom, purchase)
ecom2 <- select(ecom1, device, order_value)
ecom3 <- group_by(ecom2, device)
ecom4 <- summarise(ecom3, revenue = sum(order_value), orders = n())
ecom5 <- mutate(ecom4, aov = revenue / orders)
ecom6 <- select(ecom5, device, aov)
ecom7 <- arrange(ecom6, aov)
ecom7
```

At each step we create a new variable (data frame) and then use
it as an input in the next step; the output from one step becomes the input
for the next. Can we achieve the final outcome, `ecom7`, without creating the
intermediate data (ecom1 - ecom6)? Yes, we can. We will use the `|>` operator
to chain the steps and get rid of the intermediate data.

```{r dplyr18}
ecom |>
  filter(purchase) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(order_value), orders = n(), .by = device) |>
  mutate(
    aov = revenue / orders
  ) |>
  select(device, aov) |>
  arrange(aov)
```

Below we map the description of each step to dplyr verbs.

```{r img12, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/dplyr_aov_map.png")
```

- what is the average time on site for purchasers vs non-purchasers?
- what is the average number of pages visited by purchasers and non-purchasers using mobile?

## Try it in your browser

Edit the code below and press **Run**. It executes entirely in your browser
via [WebR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) — no R installation needed.
The runtime downloads once, on this page only.
:::

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
if (!file.exists("ecom_sample.csv")) {
  download.file(
    "https://wrangle-r.rsquaredacademy.com/data-webr/ecom_sample.csv",
    "ecom_sample.csv"
  )
}
ecom <- read_csv("ecom_sample.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ecom |>
  filter(purchase) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(order_value), orders = n(), .by = device) |>
  mutate(aov = revenue / orders) |>
  arrange(desc(aov))
```
